6e5de25d3f.q: What early career skill did a major financial executive develop through low-status sales and trading work?
6e5de25d3f.a: Bloomberg learned the meta skill of sales and the importance of actually picking up the telephone and talking to customers. He emphasized that great salespeople present everything they have and highlight whatever facts enable customers to convince themselves they are getting a good deal, a technique he would later apply to building his company.

20937c140b.q: How should an employee make themselves indispensable to advance their career?
20937c140b.a: Bloomberg came in every morning at 7 a.m., getting there before everyone else except Billy, his boss. He would stay later than anyone else and made himself available when his boss needed to borrow a match, talk sports, or make after-hours calls to big clients. At age 26, he became a buddy of the managing partner through this omnipresence and close working relationship.
f: Become physically present before everyone else and visible long after they leave —Bloomberg arrived at 7 a.m. when even his boss was still asleep, stayed later than anyone in the office, and made himself available for any request his managing partner needed. By age 26, this relentless omnipresence had turned him into a trusted confidant and set him apart from peers competing for advancement.

At Salomon Brothers in the 1970s, Bloomberg understood that career momentum comes from being the person your boss thinks of first when opportunity or crisis strikes. He didn't just show up—he showed up early enough to be there before anyone else, and he lingered long enough to handle whatever came up after hours: client calls, conversations, tasks that only a select few were trusted with.

This wasn't performative busyness. Bloomberg was solving real problems and being genuinely useful. When his managing partner Billy Salomon needed to borrow a match, discuss sports, or make important calls to major clients, Bloomberg was already there. The episode explores how this accessibility built a relationship that lasted through major career transitions, including Bloomberg's shift from sales and trading into computer systems supervision—a role his bosses asked him to take on because they trusted his judgment and work ethic completely.
"The more you work, the better you do. It's that simple. I've always outworked the other person."

Michael Bloomberg — Founder and Owner, Bloomberg. Bloomberg spent 15 years at Salomon Brothers starting as a clerk in 1966 at age 24, rising to become a close associate of managing partner Billy Salomon. After being terminated at age 39 with $10 million in compensation when Salomon Brothers was sold, he used that capital to start Bloomberg, building it into one of the world's most valuable privately held companies over 15 years.

The strategy works because it addresses a fundamental truth about advancement: your boss will promote the person they see most , trust most, and feel most confident relying on. Presence alone isn't enough—you must be present and productive, available and useful. Bloomberg did both at scale.

77e8725032.q: What is the relationship between showing up, hard work, and success in professional achievement?
77e8725032.a: Bloomberg states that eighty percent of life is just showing up, and you can control how hard you work. He believed the more you work, the better you do, and that he has always outworked the other person. If he hadn't, he or she would be writing his book.
f: Eighty percent of life is just showing up , and the other twenty percent is effort you can control. The formula is straightforward: the harder you work, the better you perform—and Bloomberg built his entire career on outworking his peers, from his early days at Salomon Brothers through founding Bloomberg.

Bloomberg's philosophy isn't abstract motivational rhetoric; it's grounded in deliberate daily practice. During his 15 years at Salomon Brothers, where he worked 12-hour days and six-day weeks, he made presence his competitive advantage. He arrived before almost everyone else each morning and stayed later, a pattern that Bloomberg discusses in detail in this episode , explaining how he became indispensable to his boss, managing partner Billy Salomon.

The consistency mattered more than occasional bursts of intensity. Bloomberg didn't view showing up as a side benefit of work—he treated it as the foundation itself. Every day counted. Every morning at the office before your competitors gave you a compounding edge over months and years.
"The more you work, the better you do. It's that simple. I've always outworked the other person."

Michael Bloomberg — Founder and Owner of Bloomberg, and former managing partner at Salomon Brothers. Bloomberg spent 15 years at Salomon Brothers starting as a clerk in 1966 at age 24, eventually becoming one of managing partner Billy Salomon's closest associates. Fired at age 39 with $10 million in severance, he invested $300,000 of that windfall to launch Bloomberg, which he built into one of the world's most valuable privately held companies within 15 years.

When Bloomberg was terminated from Salomon Brothers at age 39 following the firm's sale, he possessed something more valuable than the $10 million severance: a tested mental model that hard work compounds. He immediately deployed it as an entrepreneur. The podcast explores how Bloomberg applied this discipline to building his company from scratch , never looking back at what he'd lost, only forward at what he'd build.

f3477b44bb.q: Why should entrepreneurs avoid extensive upfront planning and five-year plans?
f3477b44bb.a: Bloomberg argued that central planning didn't work for Stalin or Mao and it won't work for an entrepreneur either. He believed you must string together many small incremental advances rather than count on hitting the lottery jackpot once, and you should constantly enhance your skills, put in many hours, make tactical plans for the next few steps, then adjust based on what actually occurs.
f: Extensive planning doesn't work for entrepreneurs any more than it worked for Stalin or Mao—success comes from stringing together many small incremental advances rather than betting on a single grand vision. Bloomberg believed you must constantly enhance your skills, put in the hours, make tactical plans for the next few steps, then adjust based on what actually happens.

The trap of five-year planning is that it assumes you can predict the future with accuracy, but reality rarely conforms to a spreadsheet . As Bloomberg describes in the episode , entrepreneurs must stay flexible and responsive. The moment you lock into an inflexible plan, you become brittle—unable to pivot when conditions change or opportunities emerge that you couldn't have anticipated.
Building through small wins, not lottery-ticket thinking

The alternative to comprehensive upfront planning is tactical iteration paired with relentless execution . Bloomberg didn't emerge from Salomon Brothers with a 15-year master plan to build a financial-information empire; he knew he wanted to start something with his $10 million severance, but his real edge came from executing small, testable moves and learning as he went. Each decision fed the next, and each failure or success informed his direction.

This mindset separates entrepreneurs who adapt from those who fail while defending their original thesis. Bloomberg's philosophy centers on the idea that you cannot outsmart the future—you can only outwork it. Small advances compound. Constant skill enhancement ensures you're prepared when opportunity arrives. And tactical short-term planning keeps you anchored in reality.
"The more you work, the better you do. It's that simple. I've always outworked the other person."

b62731bd03.q: How should a new entrepreneur validate their business idea before scaling?
b62731bd03.a: Bloomberg emphasized that a task is easier if you structure things so that you like doing them, and doing more almost always leads to greater accomplishments. He stated every significant advance his company ever made has been evolutionary rather than revolutionary—small earned steps, not big lucky hits—and they accomplished things that weren't always what they set out to do, with unforeseen uses arising for their products.
f: Validation doesn't require a perfect business plan or a big initial bet. Every significant advance comes from small, earned steps—evolutionary progress, not revolutionary leaps. Structure your work so you enjoy doing it, and unforeseen opportunities emerge naturally as you execute and learn from real market feedback.

When Michael Bloomberg left Salomon Brothers at age 39 with $10 million in compensation, he didn't spend months writing a detailed five-year business plan. Instead, he invested $300,000 to start his company and built it through iteration. His approach was deliberate: start with something concrete, test it in the real world, and adjust based on what actually works.

The validation process Bloomberg describes isn't about proving everything upfront—it's about arranging your work so momentum builds naturally. As you work harder and longer than competitors, patterns emerge. Products find uses you never anticipated. Market signals guide the next small step forward.
"The more you work, the better you do. It's that simple. I've always outworked the other person."

Michael Bloomberg — Founder and Owner of Bloomberg. Bloomberg spent 15 years at Salomon Brothers starting as a clerk counting securities in 1966 at age 24, eventually becoming a close associate of managing partner Billy Salomon. After being fired at 39 with $10 million in compensation following the firm's sale, he leveraged that capital to launch Bloomberg, building it into one of the world's most valuable privately held companies within 15 years through disciplined, incremental execution.

A key insight emerges from Bloomberg's story: validation happens through consistent execution , not through endless planning. When he started Bloomberg, he didn't know exactly how the product would evolve or which markets would value it most. But by working relentlessly and staying attuned to real customer needs, the company discovered applications and growth vectors that no spreadsheet could have predicted at the beginning.

287a80b987.q: What is the critical mindset difference between successful and unsuccessful entrepreneurs regarding risk and challenge?
287a80b987.a: Bloomberg stated that happiness for him has always been the thrill of the unknown, trying something that everyone says can't be done, and feeling that gnawing put in his stomach that says danger ahead. He said work is a very big part of his life and he loves it, waking up looking forward to getting in early, practicing his profession, creating something, and competing against the best—it is a real high to be a participant rather than a spectator.
f: Successful entrepreneurs don't flee from risk—they embrace the thrill of the unknown as the core driver of their work. Rather than viewing challenges as dangers to avoid, they experience that gnawing feeling in their stomach as a signal they're doing something genuinely hard, something most people say cannot be done. The difference isn't courage born from ignorance; it's a fundamental rewiring of how one experiences difficulty.

This mindset shift separates those who build from those who manage. When you stop treating risk as a threat and start treating it as the price of entry into meaningful work, your entire relationship with entrepreneurship transforms. The unknown stops being a source of anxiety and becomes the source of genuine excitement and engagement .

As Michael Bloomberg explains in this episode , this isn't about recklessness. It's about recognizing that being a participant in the arena—competing against the best, creating something tangible, waking up eager to practice your craft—delivers a real high that sitting safely on the sidelines can never match.
From employee to founder: learning to live with the unknown

Bloomberg's own journey illustrates this transformation starkly. After 15 years at Salomon Brothers working 12-hour days, six days a week , he was terminated at age 39 when the firm's leadership decided to push him out. He walked away with $10 million in compensation—a safety net most entrepreneurs never have—yet he chose not to retreat to comfort. Instead, he took that capital and launched Bloomberg with a $300,000 initial deposit , betting everything on a market no one yet believed in.

The critical moment wasn't the firing itself; it was what Bloomberg didn't do. He didn't look over his shoulder. He didn't visit the old firm to reminisce. As he describes in the podcast , once something was finished, it was gone—life continues forward. That psychological clean break allowed him to redirect all his energy into the unknown territory of his startup, rather than dividing his attention between two worlds.

16c8b0810b.q: What advice would an experienced entrepreneur give to someone starting a new company?
16c8b0810b.a: Bloomberg recommended thinking about what you do better than anyone else and starting a company that fills a customer need. He stated you need a vision that is affordable, practical, and fills a customer need, then go for it without worrying too much about the details and without second-guessing your creativity or overanalyzing your project's potential.

283b179900.q: How do banks and venture capitalists typically affect an entrepreneur's decision-making and company strategy?
283b179900.a: Bloomberg stated that banks and venture capitalists can be the worst enemies of entrepreneurs because they create doubt in entrepreneurs' minds and think they can help by telling the entrepreneur how to run the business. Often they kill off what's different, special, and full of potential.

663eba9c57.q: What is the optimal sequencing of business priorities when launching a startup?
663eba9c57.a: Bloomberg emphasized building the product first and thinking about accounting and shipping much later in the process. He stated that selling is the only process they run simultaneously with development from the start, prioritizing product development and sales in parallel while delaying administrative functions.
